## The problem
You want a third-party app (a calendar) to read your Google contacts without giving it your Google password. **OAuth 2.0** is a delegated **authorization** framework: the user grants an app limited, revocable access via tokens. **OpenID Connect (OIDC)** layers **authentication** on top: it tells the app who the user is.

## Roles
- Resource owner (user), Client (the app), Authorization server (issues tokens, e.g. Google, Okta), Resource server (the API)
- Scopes limit access (contacts.readonly). Access token = key to the API; refresh token = renew access; ID token (OIDC) = JWT proving the user's identity.

## Authorization Code flow with PKCE (the one to know)
Used by web apps, SPAs and mobile apps. Current best practice (OAuth 2.1 direction) for all public clients.
```
1. Client creates code_verifier (random) and code_challenge = BASE64URL(SHA256(verifier)), plus a random state
2. Redirect user to /authorize?response_type=code&client_id&redirect_uri&scope&state&code_challenge&code_challenge_method=S256
3. User logs in and consents at the authorization server
4. Redirect back to redirect_uri?code=abc&state=...   (check state matches)
5. Client POSTs to /token: code, redirect_uri, code_verifier (+ client secret for confidential clients)
6. Server checks SHA256(verifier) == challenge, returns access_token (+ refresh_token, id_token)
7. Client calls the API with Authorization: Bearer <access_token>
```
Why a code, not a token, in the redirect? Tokens in the URL leak via history and referrers. The code is useless without the verifier (PKCE), which defeats interception by malicious apps. **state** prevents CSRF on the callback.

## Other flows
- **Client Credentials**: machine-to-machine, no user; client authenticates with secret or mTLS to get a token
- **Device Code**: TVs and CLIs; show a code the user enters on another device
- **Refresh Token**: swap for a new access token; rotate on use
- **Implicit** and **Resource Owner Password**: deprecated, do not use

## OIDC
Adds the openid scope and an **ID token** (JWT with sub, iss, aud, exp, nonce, name/email claims), a /userinfo endpoint and a discovery document (/.well-known/openid-configuration) with the JWKS URL. "Sign in with Google" is OIDC. The client must validate the ID token: signature, iss, aud equals its client_id, exp, and nonce.
Key distinction: an access token is for the API (the client should treat it as opaque); the ID token is for the client, to learn who logged in. Do not use an access token as proof of login.

## Security checklist
- Exact-match redirect_uri allow-listing (open redirects leak codes)
- Always PKCE, always check state and nonce
- Short access token lifetimes, rotating refresh tokens, store refresh tokens carefully (BFF pattern: keep tokens on the server and give the SPA a session cookie)
- Request minimal scopes; allow users to revoke
- Opaque tokens with introspection (RFC 7662) vs self-contained JWT access tokens: same revocation trade-off as sessions vs JWT

## Pitfalls
- Saying OAuth is authentication.
- Putting tokens in localStorage in SPAs without considering XSS.
- Skipping audience validation, so a token for service A works on service B.
keyPoints: OAuth 2.0 delegates access with scoped tokens; OIDC adds an ID token for authentication
Authorization Code + PKCE is the standard flow for web, SPA and mobile; the code is exchanged server-side with the verifier
state defends the callback against CSRF, nonce binds the ID token to the request, redirect URIs must match exactly
Client Credentials is for machine-to-machine; Implicit and password flows are deprecated
Access token is for the API, ID token is for the client; validate iss, aud, exp and signature

security:3.body:
## The problem
When a database leaks (and eventually one does), stored passwords must not be recoverable or crackable in bulk. Never store plaintext, never encrypt reversibly, never use a fast hash.

## Why not SHA-256 / MD5
General hashes are designed to be **fast**. A modern GPU computes billions of SHA-256 hashes per second, so most human passwords fall in minutes. Rainbow tables precompute hash lookups, and identical passwords produce identical hashes, revealing duplicates.

## What password hashing adds
- **Salt**: a unique random value (16+ bytes) per password, stored beside the hash. Defeats rainbow tables and makes equal passwords hash differently. It is not secret.
- **Work factor (slowness)**: deliberately expensive, tunable computation, so each guess costs the attacker real time. Aim for roughly 100-500 ms per hash on your server, and raise it over time as hardware improves.
- **Memory hardness**: requiring lots of RAM per hash cripples GPU/ASIC parallelism.
- **Pepper** (optional): a secret key mixed in (HMAC) and held outside the database, such as in a KMS/HSM, so a database-only leak is insufficient.

## The algorithms
- **bcrypt**: 1999, Blowfish-based, cost parameter (2^cost rounds), 22-char salt built in, silently truncates input at 72 bytes. Still acceptable, widely supported, only slightly GPU-resistant, little memory use. Cost 12 or more today.
- **scrypt**: adds memory hardness.
- **Argon2id**: winner of the Password Hashing Competition (2015), currently the recommended choice. Parameters: memory, iterations, parallelism. OWASP minimum example: 19 MiB memory, 2 iterations, 1 degree of parallelism (or stronger variants such as 46 MiB, 1 iteration). Argon2id blends resistance to side-channel and GPU attacks.
- **PBKDF2**: FIPS-approved, iterations only (hundreds of thousands, OWASP suggests 600,000 for HMAC-SHA256), not memory hard; use when compliance demands it.

## Login flow
```
register: salt = random(16); hash = argon2id(password, salt, params); store "$argon2id$v=19$m=19456,t=2,p=1$salt$hash"
login:    parse stored params and salt; recompute; constant-time compare; on success, rehash if params are outdated
```
The encoded string stores algorithm, parameters and salt, so you can raise parameters later and upgrade hashes transparently at the next successful login.

## Operational considerations
- Hashing is CPU/memory intensive: it is a **DoS vector**, so rate-limit login attempts per account and IP, add progressive delays or CAPTCHA, and run hashing off the event loop in Node (use the async API or a worker pool).
- Use **constant-time comparison** to avoid timing leaks.
- Enforce length (minimum 8-12, allow up to 64+ characters), allow passphrases and password managers, check against breached-password lists (Have I Been Pwned k-anonymity API), avoid composition rules and forced periodic rotation (NIST 800-63B).
- Add MFA; offer passkeys to remove passwords entirely.
- Avoid the bcrypt 72-byte truncation trap: pre-hash long inputs carefully or use Argon2.
- Do not use the same code to hash API tokens: random 256-bit tokens can be stored as a plain SHA-256 since they have high entropy.
- Reset links: random single-use, short-lived tokens, stored hashed.

## Interview answer in one line
Hash with Argon2id (or bcrypt cost 12+) using a unique per-user salt and a tuned work factor, compare in constant time, rate-limit attempts, and upgrade parameters over time.
keyPoints: Use a slow, salted, memory-hard password hash (Argon2id preferred, bcrypt cost 12+ acceptable), never plain SHA or MD5
Salt is unique per password and not secret; it defeats rainbow tables and hides duplicates
Tune the work factor to roughly 100-500 ms and upgrade hashes at login when parameters change
Rate-limit logins since hashing is a DoS vector; compare in constant time
bcrypt truncates at 72 bytes; high-entropy API tokens can use a fast hash instead

## Why these four
They are the classic ways attackers turn untrusted input or ambient browser trust into code execution, data theft or internal access. Injection and broken access control feature in the OWASP Top 10 (2021: A01 Broken Access Control, A03 Injection, A10 SSRF; XSS now sits under Injection).

## Injection (SQL, NoSQL, OS command)
Untrusted data is concatenated into an interpreter's command, so data becomes code.
```
query = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '" + name + "'"
name = x' OR '1'='1      ->  returns every user
name = x'; DROP TABLE users; --
```
Defence:
- **Parameterised queries / prepared statements**: the query structure and data travel separately, so data can never alter the structure. This is the primary fix; escaping by hand is fragile.
- ORMs are safe unless you build raw strings with them; allow-list dynamic parts like ORDER BY columns
- NoSQL: reject objects where strings are expected ({ "$ne": null } in Mongo)
- OS commands: avoid shells; pass argv arrays, validate against an allow-list
- Least-privilege DB accounts, input validation as defence in depth

## XSS (cross-site scripting)
Attacker's script runs in a victim's browser in your origin, so it can read the DOM, steal tokens, and act as the user.
- **Stored**: payload saved (a comment) and served to others. **Reflected**: payload in a URL echoed back. **DOM-based**: client JS writes untrusted data into the page (innerHTML).
Defence:
- **Context-aware output encoding** (HTML body, attribute, JS, URL contexts differ). Frameworks like React escape by default; the danger is dangerouslySetInnerHTML, v-html, innerHTML.
- Sanitise rich text with a vetted library (DOMPurify), never regexes
- **Content-Security-Policy** limiting script sources (nonce-based, no unsafe-inline) as a second line
- HttpOnly cookies so scripts cannot read session cookies, Trusted Types

## CSRF (cross-site request forgery)
A malicious site makes the victim's browser send a request to your site, and the browser attaches the victim's cookies automatically.
```
<form action="https://bank.com/transfer" method="POST"> auto-submitted from evil.com
```
Defence:
- **SameSite cookies** (Lax by default in modern browsers; Strict for sensitive)
- **CSRF tokens**: unpredictable per-session value in a header or hidden field that the attacker's page cannot read (synchroniser or double-submit pattern)
- Check Origin / Referer headers, require custom headers for APIs (triggers CORS preflight)
- Never change state on GET; re-authenticate for sensitive actions
- APIs using Authorization: Bearer headers (not cookies) are not CSRF-prone, though they carry XSS/storage risks.
XSS beats CSRF defences, since an XSS script can read tokens, so fix XSS first.

## SSRF (server-side request forgery)
The server fetches a URL supplied by the user (webhooks, image fetch, PDF render, URL preview), and the attacker aims it at internal targets.
```
url=http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/   -> cloud credentials
url=http://localhost:6379/                                              -> internal Redis
```
The 2019 Capital One breach involved SSRF against the AWS metadata service.
Defence:
- Allow-list destination hosts/schemes where possible; otherwise resolve DNS and **block private, loopback, link-local (169.254.0.0/16) and metadata ranges**, re-check after redirects, and defend against DNS rebinding by connecting to the resolved IP
- Disable unneeded schemes (file://, gopher://) and redirects
- Use IMDSv2 (session-token based) on AWS; network egress controls; run fetchers in an isolated network segment with no credentials

## Interview pattern
For each: what is the trust failure, a payload, the root fix, and the defence in depth. Root fixes are parameterisation, output encoding, SameSite plus tokens, and destination allow-listing.
keyPoints: Injection: separate code from data with parameterised queries; avoid shells and raw string building
XSS: encode output by context, avoid innerHTML-style sinks, sanitise rich text, add CSP and HttpOnly cookies
CSRF abuses automatic cookies: use SameSite, anti-CSRF tokens, Origin checks, and no state change on GET
SSRF: allow-list or block private, loopback and metadata IPs, re-check redirects and DNS, use IMDSv2
Always name the root cause and the primary fix, then defence in depth

security:5.body:
## The problem
Applications need credentials (DB passwords, API keys, signing keys), and data needs protecting both where it sits and while it moves. Leaked secrets in git history and unencrypted backups are among the most common real breaches.

## Secrets management
Rules:
- **Never** commit secrets to git, bake them into images, or log them. Scanning tools (gitleaks, trufflehog, GitHub secret scanning) catch accidents; if one leaks, **rotate it**, since deleting the commit is not enough.
- Separate secrets from config; inject at runtime
- Least privilege and per-service identities, so one leak does not expose everything
Options, from basic to strong:
- Environment variables: simple, but visible to child processes, crash dumps and sometimes /proc; acceptable for small apps
- Platform stores: AWS Secrets Manager / SSM Parameter Store, GCP Secret Manager, Azure Key Vault, Kubernetes Secrets (base64 only; enable encryption at rest in etcd, or use external-secrets/CSI drivers)
- **HashiCorp Vault**: central store, fine-grained policies, audit log, **dynamic secrets** (short-lived DB credentials generated per client and auto-revoked), transit encryption as a service
- Prefer **workload identity** (IAM roles, OIDC federation, SPIFFE) so there is no long-lived secret at all
Operational: automated rotation (for example 30-90 days or shorter), versioning with rollback, audit trails on access, break-glass procedure, separate secrets per environment.

## Encryption at rest
Protects against stolen disks, snapshots and backups, but not against a compromised application with valid access.
- Symmetric AES-256 (GCM)
- **Envelope encryption**: data encrypted with a unique data key (DEK); the DEK is encrypted with a master key (KEK) held in a KMS/HSM. Only small keys go to the KMS, the master key never leaves it, rotating the KEK means re-wrapping DEKs, not re-encrypting all data.
```
plaintext --AES-GCM(DEK)--> ciphertext ;  DEK --KMS(KEK)--> wrapped DEK (stored beside ciphertext)
```
- Levels: full-disk, database TDE, per-object or per-field/column (application-level) encryption for especially sensitive data (the DB admin cannot read it), client-side encryption
- Key management is the real problem: who can call decrypt, key rotation, backup, audit. Encrypting data with a key stored next to it adds nothing.

## Encryption in transit
- **TLS 1.2+ (prefer 1.3)** everywhere, including internal service traffic; **mTLS** between services for mutual identity (service meshes automate rotation)
- HSTS to prevent downgrade, valid certificates with automated renewal, disable old protocols and weak ciphers
- Database and cache connections should also use TLS; VPN or private links for cross-site traffic
- Do not rely on "it is inside the VPC" as the sole control

## End-to-end encryption
Only endpoints hold keys (Signal, WhatsApp), so the server cannot read content. Trade-off: server-side search, moderation and recovery become hard.

## Hashing vs encryption vs encoding
Hash: one-way (passwords, integrity). Encryption: reversible with a key (confidentiality). Encoding (base64): neither, just format. Signing (HMAC or digital signatures): integrity and authenticity.

## Pitfalls
- Base64 or XOR called "encryption", rolling your own crypto, ECB mode, hard-coded keys, reused IVs/nonces with GCM.
- Rotating a secret without a dual-valid overlap window, causing outages.
- Secrets in CI logs, client-side bundles (NEXT_PUBLIC_ variables are public) and error messages.
keyPoints: Keep secrets out of git and logs, inject at runtime from a secret store, rotate on any leak, prefer workload identity
Vault-style dynamic secrets give short-lived, per-client credentials with audit trails
Envelope encryption: data key encrypts data, KMS-held master key wraps the data key; rotate by re-wrapping
Encrypt in transit with TLS 1.2+/1.3 and mTLS internally; do not trust the internal network
Hash, encrypt, encode and sign are different tools; never roll your own crypto or reuse GCM nonces
